item.title: Babyface Ray Calls Out Guns, Cups And Pills On “Big Facts”
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Babyface Ray criticized the chase for guns, cups and pills on "Big Facts," while discussing fatherhood and his career.
item.content:encoded:
Babyface Ray questioned the appeal of guns, cups and pills to younger people in a new “Big Facts” interview.

The episode, released November 3, also found the Detroit rapper discussing the demands of raising children while making music.

“Like, everybody just zombied out. They want a gun. They want a cup. And they want a perk,” Ray said.

The rapper said he had seven children and spoke about balancing his career with fatherhood, being present for his children and staying busy.

He said his children looked to him and gave him reason to keep going. He had also collected footage for a documentary, without announcing a title or release date.

Ray had discussed his own history with pills and lean years before those comments. In a 2022 Detroit Metro Times profile, he described using them to cope after his son was stillborn.

The loss came during a difficult period when he felt caught between music and the streets, and he said it left him questioning his faith.

“I was in a dark, dark place,” Ray said in that earlier interview.

He also recalled concern about how others would react to his choices: “I was scared of what people would think of the decisions I would make.”

He described refocusing on his life and music after that period. Those comments appeared in a profile tied to his 2022 album FACE.

More recently, his work with Lelo put him alongside a younger Detroit rapper seeking advice beyond music.

In a joint interview with The FADER in June, Lelo said he called Ray with questions about investments and real estate. Ray had brought him out at Racket in New York on June 9, during a tour with 42 Dugg and Jorjiana.

The connection ran through 4amjuno, who engineered for Ray and produced for Lelo. He introduced Ray to “On The Wall,” and Ray joined the record after hearing it at a home recording session.

Ray described a change in Detroit rap, from songs rooted in the local environment to music with a wider audience.

He said, “Now I think it’s more sauce and swag to it, so it’s more relatable to the world.”

item.title: Yung Miami Says She Is Focused On Herself After Diddy Backlash
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Yung Miami says she is focused on herself as she revisits the criticism surrounding her former relationship with Sean Combs.
item.content:encoded:
Yung Miami is putting herself first after another round of questions about her private life and her former relationship with Sean “Diddy” Combs.

During the November 4 installment of The Jason Lee Show, the Miami rapper addressed whether she is single and the criticism that has followed her connection to Combs. BET’s summary of the conversation says she ultimately decided to focus on herself.

The conversation also lands during a major solo reset. Her debut album, Watch Dis!, arrived in October and turned the end of City Girls, her fractured bond with JT and the Combs fallout into part of the music. The interview gives her room to draw a line between that history and what comes next.

The answer arrives after months of Yung Miami explaining why she will not let public pressure rewrite what she experienced. The relationship ended in 2023, but the scrutiny continued through Combs’ federal case and her decision to ask for leniency before his sentencing.

She has also been blunt about the cost. “I lost deals. I lost money. I lost relationships. I lost a lot,” she said during a March interview.

That earlier conversation made clear that her loyalty came with consequences.

“I can only judge a person off of what I know and what I experience,” she told The Breakfast Club. She also acknowledged that the fallout damaged her brand and narrowed the circle of people she trusted.

“The only person I try to trust is God and my kids,” she said in the same interview. Her latest answer on BET sounds like an extension of that boundary, with less attention on proving anything to the public and more on protecting her own peace.

The legal record remains separate from her personal account. Combs was convicted of two transportation-to-engage-in-prostitution counts and acquitted of racketeering and sex-trafficking charges. He received a 50-month prison sentence and is serving his time at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey.

Yung Miami has never claimed that her experience settles what happened to anyone else. She says she can only describe the relationship she lived, even as critics argue her support carries weight because of her public platform.

The new interview does not erase that debate. It does show where she says her energy is going now: away from defending a finished relationship and toward herself, her children and the next chapter of her work.

item.title: BigXthaPlug Says Country Artists Have The Unity Hip-Hop Lacks
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: BigXthaPlug praised the friendships he found in country music and compared them with the divisions he saw among rappers.
item.content:encoded:
BigXthaPlug said country artists made more room for real friendships than rappers did, pointing to the time they spent together away from work.

On the October 28 episode of “Club Shay Shay,” Shannon Sharpe asked the Dallas rapper about unity across the two genres. BigX described a Hip-Hop scene divided by cities, naming Atlanta, Miami and New York as examples of separate rap circles.

“the difference with a country artist is that you can catch those two artists drinking beer at a bar on a random Wednesday, just cause,” BigX said.

He contrasted that with rap gatherings he believed were arranged by labels rather than built on friendships away from work. He also described a more relaxed backstage experience at Stagecoach than Rolling Loud.

Those relationships helped shape I Hope You’re Happy, his country project released in August 2025. Luke Combs and Jelly Roll supported him before he committed to making the record.

Combs connected with BigX after a sold-out Houston show and expressed interest in working together. Their friendship even extended to watches, with Combs’ collection influencing what BigX bought. As more artists learned about the country project, BigX received demos and chose songs that connected with what he was feeling.

In a separate MusicRow interview around that album’s release, he explained why his move into country did not require him to change his identity.

“Because I’m not changing what I do. The inspiration might be different, but my voice and my storytelling are still there,” he said.

The album paired him with Bailey Zimmerman on “All the Way,” Combs on “Pray Hard” and Shaboozey on “Home.” Asked about his fans, BigX said, “They’re supporting it 100%.” His own heartbreak during the recording process helped him understand the country material and gave him a way to finish the project.

His recent work kept him connected to rap collaborators as well. He gave Dallas fans an early listen to Better Over Time on October 26, pairing the new music with a short film screening.

The 18-song album was released on October 30. Lil Yachty, GloRilla, Leon Thomas and Babyface Ray were among its collaborators, giving BigX another chance to work with artists from across the rap scene.

item.title: Cam’ron And Ma$e Ask If New York’s Accent Is Disappearing
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Cam'ron and Ma$e asked whether New York's accent is disappearing as linguists tracked how younger speakers and newcomers reshape it.
item.content:encoded:
Cam’ron and Ma$e turned a question about New York’s changing voice into a full Harlem debate: Is the city’s accent slowly disappearing?

The discussion surfaced on the November 5 episode of It Is What It Is. Treasure “Stat Baby” Wilson put the question to the two rappers, whose voices, slang and comic timing carry decades of Harlem into a show built around sports and barbershop conversation.

It sounded like a casual topic, but the question has been sitting in front of New Yorkers all year. A February survey ranked New York City No. 12 among American cities where residents hear less of the local accent in everyday conversation.

That does not mean the sound is gone. It means the old markers are harder to hear as neighborhoods, schools and workplaces keep changing.

Dr. Gail August, chair of language and cognition at Hostos Community College, told ABC7 New York that some people want “the opportunities that come with standard speaking.” The station also recalled Brooklyn students taking speech classes in 2005 to sound less like New Yorkers.

Cam’ron and Ma$e make the debate more than a pronunciation exercise. Their reunion on It Is What It Is turned two distinct Harlem voices into a media business with national reach.

The show works because the hosts don’t sand away where they came from, even when the conversation moves from basketball to language.

New York rap has always carried neighborhood speech into the wider culture. If younger speakers are changing those cues, the music and media built from them will change too.

New York has never had one single accent, and none of its versions stayed frozen. Immigration, migration, class pressure and social media all push the sound in new directions.

The question Cam’ron and Ma$e raised is really whether the next version will still be recognizable when it answers back.

item.title: Stevie Wonder’s Ex Seeks Court-Ordered Repairs In Eviction Fight
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Carmen Efferson asks a court to order Stevie Wonder to repair alleged mold, plumbing, electrical and structural problems.
item.content:encoded:
Carmen Efferson has answered Stevie Wonder’s eviction lawsuit with a demand of her own.

She wants the court to make the singer repair the Los Angeles home where she has lived since 1988.

TMZ reported that Efferson denied Wonder’s claims and said the house has urgent mold, plumbing, electrical and structural problems.

She wants the judge to order repairs as part of her response to his bid to remove her. Her filing brings the condition of the home into a fight that had focused on access, insurance and an old oral deal.

Wonder sued Efferson in Los Angeles Superior Court.

His complaint said she had lived in the home without paying monthly rent since July 1988. It said the dispute grew after she refused to let his team enter for an inspection.

The stated reason was “for purposes of updating and retaining property insurance on the Premises.”

Wonder’s lawyers sent Efferson a 30-day notice on July 28, the complaint said. They sent a three-day notice on October 6 after she still had not allowed an inspection, according to his side.

That notice said, “Owner has been prejudiced by the cancellation of the property insurance policy.”

The singer asked the court to end the oral deal and return the home to him. He also sought legal fees and up to $600 in statutory damages.

Efferson’s response rejects the account in the complaint. She says Wonder should have to fix the home where she has lived for almost four decades.

Her claims about mold and the other problems are allegations in her filing. The court has not treated them as proven facts.

The two sides also tell different stories about what Wonder promised when Efferson moved in. Before she filed her response, she said he had pushed her to take the property.

“I didn’t even want the house at first, but he kept insisting,” she told the Daily Mail.

AllHipHop previously reported that Efferson called Wonder a “gaslighter and a manipulator.”

She also said she paid for major work after the 1994 Northridge earthquake and later flooding. In her account, their oral deal was meant to end with the home becoming hers.

Wonder’s complaint describes a different deal. It says she had permission to live there without rent, but it does not give her ownership. The filing also said the home had been uninsured since August 4.

The case now has two competing sets of claims.

Wonder says Efferson blocked the inspection needed to protect the property. Efferson denies his case and says he should be ordered to make urgent repairs while he seeks to take back the home.

item.title: Terrence Howard Predicts AI Will End Hollywood’s Traditional Industry Model
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Terrence Howard says AI will close Hollywood's golden age as his new thriller "A Good Hand Wasted" heads to Turnstr+.
item.content:encoded:
Terrence Howard believes artificial intelligence will end Hollywood’s traditional industry model, TMZ reported.

He made the remarks at an event for his new film, “A Good Hand Wasted.”

The “Empire” star described Hollywood’s golden age as nearing its close, but he did not present that shift as entirely bad.

His prediction lands in an industry already trying to decide whether AI will remain another production tool or remake how movies are financed, staffed and created.

Major studios are weighing faster, cheaper production against jobs and copyright concerns. Google has also explored licensing agreements with Hollywood companies for its AI tools.

The fight is not only about what studios can generate.

It is also about who controls an actor’s face, voice and performance. SAG-AFTRA’s latest agreement separates authorized digital replicas from fully synthetic creations, putting consent at the center of the debate.

In a separate industry discussion, director Ron Howard argued that audiences will decide whether AI-made films succeed and suggested traditional and AI-assisted production could coexist.

His view is less absolute than Terrence Howard’s forecast and shows how unsettled the industry’s debate remains.

Terrence Howard delivered his remarks as “A Good Hand Wasted” prepared for its November 6 premiere on Turnstr+.

The psychological thriller follows six longtime friends whose private-island vacation turns dangerous after they are pulled into a high-stakes poker game, according to a report on the film.

The setup puts their loyalty and survival on the table as the game closes around them.

That story gives Howard a timely backdrop for talking about risk and an industry in transition. He also framed the movie’s message in more personal terms. “Hopefully, the audience will learn to appreciate living in the moment,” Howard said.

He followed with another direct thought about what he hopes viewers carry away from the film: “Life is supposed to be lived and appreciated, not taken for granted.”

Rhyan Lamarr wrote and directed “A Good Hand Wasted” and also worked on its music. The movie is part of Lamarr’s three-picture agreement with Turnstr+ and arrives later that week, as Howard comments on the business facing the end of an era.

item.title: YFG Fatso Waives Extradition To Georgia After Chicago Hearing
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: YFG Fatso waived extradition to Georgia after a Chicago hearing, a report said. The underlying Georgia offense was not identified.
item.content:encoded:
YFG Fatso waived extradition to Georgia at a November 2 hearing in Chicago, according to Chicago Crime Chaser, which reported that the rapper faced a warrant from that state.

The 19-year-old artist, whose legal name is Christopher C. Mosley, was booked in Cook County on October 29 on a local fugitive hold tied to the Georgia warrant.

Judge Rivanda Doss Beal handled the hearing at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse. The report said local prosecutors dropped the fugitive hold, but a custody order kept him awaiting pickup by Georgia authorities.

The account did not identify the underlying Georgia offense or establish that a transfer had taken place. It also did not say where he was.

Fatso had discussed an earlier period of house arrest on “Off The Porch.” The October 2025 episode description said he had recently come off house arrest then. That account preceded this week’s extradition proceedings by more than a year.

That appearance also covered making his first song at 13 and getting attention from the video for “Go Go.” He discussed his first connection to Lil Durk through Lil King and signing with OTF.

His album Sanity Evaded arrived July 9 through YFG Fatso/Santa Anna, following 2024’s A Reaper’s Ceremony.

The 18-song release ran 53 minutes and featured Rob49 on “Clean Up Crew” and Tee Grizzley on “They Need Me.”

item.title: Jeffrey Wright Calls W.E.B. Du Bois Documentary One Of His Proudest Projects
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Jeffrey Wright calls W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel With A Cause one of his proudest projects as Rita Coburn's documentary tours.
item.content:encoded:
Jeffrey Wright is placing his work on W.E.B. Du Bois: Rebel With A Cause among the projects that mean the most to him as Rita Coburn’s documentary continues its screening tour.

“I do a lot of stuff, but I’m not prouder of any other piece that I’ve been a part of than this,” Wright said during a conversation about the film.

Wright performs dramatic readings from Du Bois’ writing in the two-hour American Masters documentary. Viola Davis narrates, while Common and Courtney B. Vance also give voice to Du Bois’ words.

The role asked Wright to serve the language rather than turn the scholar into a character.

Coburn built the film around Du Bois’ books, speeches, journalism, archival audio and the voices of historians who explain why his work still lands.

Wright said the finished movie exceeded what he expected.

“I watched it and was just blown away by the beauty of the film and by the comprehensiveness of the narrative arc,” he told People earlier this year.

The film follows Du Bois from his 1868 birth in Massachusetts through the collapse of Reconstruction, two world wars and the rise of the modern Civil Rights Movement.

He co-founded the NAACP, helped launch the Niagara Movement and used scholarship, journalism and data to expose racial inequality.

Du Bois also challenged Booker T. Washington and Marcus Garvey, and his 1903 book The Souls of Black Folk delivered the warning that “the problem of the twentieth century is the color line.”

Coburn’s film does not flatten that history into a victory lap. It covers his political battles, internationalism and personal losses, including the death of his infant son.

Du Bois died in Ghana on August 27, 1963, one day before the March on Washington.

“My hope is that this documentary invites reflection and sparks dialogue, not only about who Du Bois was,” Coburn said on the official film page.

The documentary premiered on PBS in May and later traveled to theaters and community screenings.

A London event in October paired the movie with a conversation featuring Coburn and Wright. Screenings in Los Angeles and New York are scheduled for November 12 and November 19.

For Wright, the project connects a foundational Black thinker to the present without sanding down the force of his ideas. His pride comes from helping Du Bois’ own words remain the center of the story.

item.title: Kodak Black Likeness Appears In New GTA VI Launch Gallery
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Kodak Black appears in Rockstar's new GTA VI launch gallery, though the studio has not identified his apparent character.
item.content:encoded:
Kodak Black appears to have entered Leonida, with his likeness turning up in Rockstar Games’ new Grand Theft Auto VI launch gallery.

Rockstar released the collection Thursday (November 5), exactly two weeks before the game arrives on November 19. “Grand Theft Auto VI is now officially only two weeks away,” the company said in its announcement.

Viewers quickly zeroed in on one figure whose face tattoos, hair and 1800 Block chain closely resemble the Pompano Beach rapper. The details immediately led to claims that the image shows Kodak rather than a loose parody or an unrelated character.

An important line still exists between recognition and confirmation. Rockstar’s gallery does not name the figure.

The company has not announced whether Kodak voices anyone, appears as himself, plays a fictional character or is part of a single scene. Kodak Black has not publicly spelled out his role either.

Rockstar has kept much of the game’s voice cast secret, which makes the missing credit meaningful rather than conclusive.

His connection to the game is not coming out of nowhere. Kodak’s older music was previously confirmed for GTA VI, putting his voice in the game’s Florida-inspired world before the new image surfaced. Rockstar has also leaned heavily into regional music and culture while building Vice City and the wider state of Leonida.

The music rollout is a separate piece of that world. Rockstar announced a 34-track album of new music for launch day, with early singles from Future and Metro Boomin, Travis Scott, PinkPantheress, Rauw Alejandro, Morgan Wallen and Keith Richards. That announcement did not describe Kodak’s apparent on-screen presence.

The gallery arrives after a quieter legal stretch for Kodak, whose real name is Bill Kapri. In September, Florida prosecutors declined to file charges in an Orange County MDMA case, saying the evidence was insufficient to prove possession.

A Broward judge also dismissed a separate fleeing-and-eluding charge that month.

For now, the launch gallery supports a careful conclusion: a figure designed to look like Kodak Black is in Rockstar’s official GTA VI imagery. The size and nature of his role remain undisclosed ahead of the November 19 release.

item.title: Carmelo Anthony, La La Reportedly Reach Divorce Settlement After 9 Years
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony reportedly reached a settlement in their divorce case more than five years after the filing.
item.content:encoded:
Carmelo Anthony and La La Anthony have reportedly taken a major step toward closing a divorce case that has stretched on for more than nine years.

According to court records cited by TMZ, the former couple informed the court that they had reached a settlement.

The available report did not disclose the terms or say that a judge had entered a final divorce judgment.

That distinction matters. A reported settlement can resolve the issues between the parties, but it is not the same as confirmation that the marriage has been legally dissolved.

For now, the supported development is that Carmelo and La La appear to have worked out an agreement after a long-running case.

La La filed for divorce in June 2021 after 11 years of marriage. The filing followed years of strain.

They separated in 2017, appeared to reconcile in 2018 and later moved toward ending the marriage. They share a son, Kiyan Anthony.

By the time La La filed, she had already been living with the emotional fallout of the separation for years.

During a 2021 appearance on “The Angie Martinez Show,” she described the split as painful and public while saying she and Carmelo had reached a good place as co-parents.

She also sounded deeply uncertain about marrying again.

“Marriage, I don’t think I can do that ever again. I mean, some amazing person would have to come. I don’t see that happening again,” La La said.

The timeline helps explain why the reported settlement is significant. The public divorce filing came four years after their first separation, and the case then remained unresolved for more than five additional years.

Their ability to co-parent amicably did not mean the legal process had reached its end.

The divorce was still part of La La’s public conversation days before the settlement report.

Neither the limited settlement report nor the available court-record summary provided financial terms, parenting terms or a date for a final judgment.

It also did not include a new public statement from Carmelo or La La.

That leaves the case’s final status unclear, even with an agreement reportedly in place.

What the new report does show is movement in a case that had remained open since La La’s 2021 filing.

Until a final judgment is confirmed, the settlement should be described as a reported agreement, not a completed divorce.
